name: Freya Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Freya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and this conversation is confidential. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What's a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Ledgerline, an online accounting firm where most of us work from home. My clients are online shops and a few small app companies, so it's monthly accounts, VAT returns and the founders' own tax returns. Most mornings I'm reviewing what the AI tools have already prepared overnight and fixing the bits they got wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy building things. Last year I wrote the instructions our AI tool follows for month-end, and it cut about two days off each client's close, which means finishing the monthly books. What wears me out is founders who send me 300 receipts as phone photos on the last day. I share a flat with my friend Corinne, and she says I narrate VAT rules while cooking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools were useful but oversold, and that the firms who used them well still got ahead. At work I'd keep improving our month-end setup. Online I'd post a short thread on what actually worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's comfortable. I'm well paid, I've got about ten months saved plus some shares, and I'd keep my edge because I use the tools more than most. Even if AI is mostly hype, I'd still be the person at my firm who gets month-end done in half the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and ask for a raise based on the hours my setup saved. I'd put more into my share account, maybe £500 a month. I might pick up two or three private clients on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little bored by the thought. I like a bit of change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would worry you even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ledgerline is growing fast on investor money, so if growth slows, they might cut staff. I'd be fine finding another job, there are plenty around. It's more annoying than scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the private clients be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably friends of friends who run small online shops. Simple accounts, a few hours a month each, done in the evenings with my own tools.

say: The AI tools were **useful but oversold**.
Firms that used them well **still got ahead**, and I'd post what actually worked.
think: I'm **well paid** with ten months saved and some shares.
I'd keep **my edge**, because I use the tools more than most.
do: Ask for a **raise** based on the hours her month-end setup saved.
Put about **£500 a month** into her share account.
Take on two or three **private clients** in the evenings.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **bored** by the idea.
S0.quote: Even if AI is mostly hype, I'd still be the person at my firm who gets month-end done in half the time.
fieldNote: Freya is **secure** in both money and skills, and sees the tools as her edge.
Her only existing worry is a **fast-growing employer** that could cut staff if growth slows.
She'd use a quiet world to build **side income**, which fits her appetite for risk.

steps.text: Ask Ledgerline for a raise based on month-end hours saved
Put £500 a month into her share account
Take on two or three online-shop clients in the evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is our moment, because we're already set up for it. To friends I'd say learn the tools now, don't wait. I'd probably post a guide for other accountants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I come out ahead in this one. The routine checking goes, but someone has to design and check what the AI does, and that's already what I do. I don't think AI takes my accounting job; it takes the job of the accountant who won't use AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to lead automation for the whole firm and get it into my title and pay. I'd add more private clients, maybe ten, because I can serve them quickly with my own setup. And I'd keep investing, because I'd expect the firm's revenue to grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited. Like the rules of a game changing in a way that suits how I play.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bookkeepers who only do data entry. There are about eight of them, and their work is exactly what the card says goes. I'd try to train the ones who want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you're too confident?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I've already watched the tools change my own job twice in two years, and I adapted both times. I'd rather be early and wrong than late and right.

say: This is **our moment**, because we're already set up for AI.
Learn the tools **now** instead of waiting.
think: I come out **ahead**, because I already design and check what the AI does.
AI replaces the accountant who **won't use it**, not me.
do: Ask to **lead automation** for the whole firm, with title and pay to match.
Grow to about **ten private clients** using her own setup.
Keep **investing** as she expects the firm's revenue to grow.
S1.quote: I don't think AI takes my accounting job; it takes the job of the accountant who won't use AI.
fieldNote: Freya expects her own job to **grow**, since she already does the work AI creates.
She worries for the **data-entry bookkeepers**, and offers to train them.
She admits she might be **overconfident**, but trusts her record of adapting twice.

steps.text: Lead Ledgerline's automation work with a new title and pay
Grow her evening practice to about ten online-shop clients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to hit accountants hard and fast, and that we should stop pretending otherwise. At work I'd say we need a plan this month, not next year. Online I'd post honestly about what I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, being good with the tools buys me a year, maybe two. Once AI can do almost any thinking work, it can also set itself up, so my month-end instructions aren't special anymore. My skill was teaching the AI to do accounts, and in two years the AI won't need teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first months selling my month-end setup to other small firms, while it's still worth something. I'd save hard, maybe half my pay, and stop buying shares until things settle. By 2028 I'd want a job that needs a person, maybe running the finance side of a business with real premises, like a bike shop or a gym.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have a plan by the end of the week. That's how I cope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a business with real premises?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the robots are about three years behind the AI. A gym or a shop still needs people on the floor until 2031 or later. I could do the money side and help on the floor too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Corinne?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm fine for money, which is true, and that I'm going to be weird and busy for a while. She works in hospitality, so she'd probably have more time than me in this one.

say: This hits **accountants hard and fast**, so stop pretending.
Firms need a plan **this month**, not next year.
think: Being good with the tools buys me **a year or two** at most.
Once AI can **set itself up**, my month-end skills aren't special anymore.
do: Sell her **month-end setup** to other small firms while it still has value.
Save about **half her pay** and pause share buying.
Move into **finance for a business** with premises, like a gym or shop.
feel: **Anxious**, but calmer once she has a **plan**.
S2.quote: My skill was teaching the AI to do accounts, and in two years the AI won't need teaching.
fieldNote: Freya sees that being **ahead on AI** stops protecting her once AI can set itself up.
She'd **cash in** on her skills fast, then move toward hands-on businesses.
Her mood is anxious, not alarmed, because of her **savings** and a ready plan.

steps.text: Sell her AI month-end setup to other small accounting firms
Save half her pay and pause buying shares
Apply to run finances for a gym or bike shop by 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to do this properly, and I'd tell people to start now. At work I'd push for training budgets for everyone, not just me. I'd post about the career paths I'm looking at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a good window for me. I'd get maybe three good years from AI skills, then switch before 2031. Five years of warning means I can make money from AI first and then get out of its way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd build my evening practice up to fifteen clients and save the extra. Year two or three, I'd look at buying into a small business with premises, maybe a climbing gym, since I climb three times a week. I'd keep a year of costs in cash throughout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared. It's a big puzzle, and I like puzzles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A climbing gym is a big step for an accountant. Would you really do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to work there part-time first and see the numbers. But yes, I'd seriously consider it. I already know the owner of mine, and she's talked about selling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the robots come to the climbing gym too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have had three good years and learned how to run a business. That's still more than I'd have sitting at home reviewing AI-made accounts.

say: Five years is **long enough** to do this properly.
Everyone should get a **training budget**, not just the keen ones.
think: I'd get about **three good years** from AI skills before switching.
I can **make money from AI** first, then get out of its way.
do: Build the evening practice to **fifteen clients** and save the extra.
Work part-time at her **climbing gym**, then consider buying in.
Keep **a year of costs** in cash throughout.
S3.quote: Five years of warning means I can make money from AI first and then get out of its way.
fieldNote: With five years, Freya sees a **window to profit** before her desk work goes.
Her move toward a **climbing gym** comes from her own hobby and its later robot date.
She frames the whole thing as a **puzzle**, which fits her adaptive nature.

steps.text: Grow the evening accounting practice to fifteen clients
Work part-time at the climbing gym, then consider buying in
Keep a full year of living costs in cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty and the people who plan will be fine. At work I'd say let's build the best AI accounting service around while it's still a business. Online I'd post a long-term plan and probably get mocked for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is great for me. I'd earn well from AI skills for seven or eight years, save a lot and switch on my own terms. I'd be 37 when AGI arrives, with a decade of savings and a business, which is a good age to start again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start my own small accounting practice within two years, built on AI from day one. I'd invest the profits in shares and maybe a small flat. By about year six I'd start shifting into something with premises and people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. It's the version where planning really pays off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You expect your accounting work to end by 2036. Why calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the next eight years look really good for me, and I've got time to set up the next thing. I'd rather know the end date than be surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you nervous in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I got lazy and comfortable. Ten years is long enough to forget there's a deadline.

say: Ten years is **plenty**, and people who **plan** will be fine.
Let's build the **best AI accounting service** while it's still a business.
think: I'd earn well from **AI skills** for seven or eight years.
At **37**, with savings and a business, I'd be ready to **start again**.
do: Start her **own accounting practice** built on AI within two years.
Invest profits in **shares** and maybe a small flat.
Shift toward a business with **premises and people** by year six.
S4.quote: I'd be 37 when AGI arrives, with a decade of savings and a business, which is a good age to start again.
fieldNote: Freya expects the **next eight years** to be good for her, so she's calm despite the end date.
Her only fear is getting **comfortable** and forgetting the deadline.
She'd go **independent**, which suits her risk appetite and strong savings.

steps.text: Open her own AI-run accounting practice within two years
Run the new practice on AI tools from day one
Put practice profits into shares and a small flat

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my edge disappears quickly and everyone's scrambling at once. What would help is easy access to small business loans and short courses, so people like me can move into businesses with real premises quickly. I don't need handouts, I need the door open.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether people like me feel guilty. I built the AI setup that made our firm's bookkeepers less needed, and I do think about that. I'd still do it, but I'd want them to get the same training I got.

headlineQuote: I built the AI setup that made our firm's bookkeepers less needed, and I do think about that.
portrait: Freya is a **27-year-old accountant** at an online firm who builds the AI setups others use.
She rents with her friend Corinne and has **ten months saved** plus shares.
She's **calm** in the slow pictures, expecting her skills to keep her ahead.
Under **AGI by 2028**, she knows her edge fades fast but has a plan within a week.
Given time, she'd go **independent** and move toward a business with premises, like a climbing gym.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her edge would disappear while everyone scrambles.
whatWouldHelp: Easy **small business loans** and short courses, so people can move quickly.
